Final models retrained on complete training set and evaluated on independent test set to assess generalization
Effluent COD prediction achieved high accuracy across all three models with predictions tightly clustering around 1:1 line
RF demonstrated most stable COD performance with symmetric residuals around zero across the effluent COD range
XGBoost achieved similar R2 = 0.96 for COD but showed larger deviations at higher COD values indicating reduced stability under extreme loading
ANN exhibited wider prediction spread for COD at mid-to-high levels reflecting lower sensitivity to nonlinear trends
TMP prediction is challenging due to nonlinear, dynamic, and time-dependent processes (biological activity, EPS accumulation, cake layer, physicochemical)
RF achieved best TMP prediction performance (R2 = 0.88, RMSE = 3.86 kPa) aligning closely with 1:1 line
XGBoost and ANN yielded weaker generalization for TMP (R2 = 0.56, RMSE = 7.50 kPa and R2 = 0.54, RMSE = 7.59 kPa)
XGBoost exhibited overfitting on TMP (close fit to training data, large deviations on test set)
ANN showed dispersed TMP predictions indicating limited capacity to capture nonlinear fouling response
Residual analysis confirmed RF had most compact TMP residual distribution, with higher deviations at high TMP magnitudes
Residual spread was greater for TMP than effluent COD, confirming fouling prediction is more uncertain than COD prediction
Effluent COD (R2 > 0.90) is more predictable than TMP (R2 = 0.80-0.50 / 0.54-0.88) due to deterministic kinetics vs stochastic fouling
RF is best suited for COD monitoring; ANN provides robustness for TMP under variable loading; XGBoost poor TMP generalization highlights need for test-set validation
Combination of predicted-versus-observed plots and residual analysis provides comprehensive assessment
Chronological data splitting evaluated extrapolation under unseen shock-loading conditions (Phase I-II: 103 samples train; Phase III: 16 samples test)
Phase III shock-loading test resulted in negative R2 values across all models, performing worse than simple mean prediction
High random-split 80:20 performance represents strong interpolation ability rather than robust extrapolation capacity
